sections.title: Footings on Structural Fills
sections.summary: Settlement within compacted structural fills is estimated using the Hough method with an assumed corrected N' = 32 blows/ft, corresponding to approximately 85% relative density and 95% relative compaction at 100 kPa overburden. Settlement of embankment foundation soils below the fill must also be checked separately.
sections.body:
Calculation of settlement within the structural fill due to a spread footing supported in the fill requires an assumption about the compressibility of the constructed fill material. Because structural fills should be constructed using good-quality granular materials, the estimation of settlement lends itself to application of the methods discussed in the previous section (Hough and D'Appolonia methods). To do so, an assumption must be made about the representative SPT N-value of the compacted fill.

The Gifford et al. (1987) study used a corrected (for overburden pressure) SPT N-value of 32 blows per foot as a representative value for estimating settlement in structural fills. This would correspond to a relative density, D_R, of about 85 percent at an overburden stress of about 100 kPa (1 tsf). Correlations of relative density to percent relative compaction suggest that this value of D_R is at or above 95 percent relative compaction. In the absence of other SPT data in structural fills, the settlement of a footing supported on structural fill can be estimated using an assumed corrected N-value (N') of 32 and the Hough method for computing settlement.
key_points: Use Hough or D'Appolonia methods with assumed SPT N-value for compacted fill
Default assumption: corrected N' = 32 blows/ft for well-compacted structural fills
N' = 32 corresponds to D_R ~ 85% at 100 kPa overburden, equivalent to ~95% relative compaction
Fill should be good-quality granular material with sand- and gravel-sized particles
Also need to check settlement of embankment foundation soils below the fill
sections.applicability: Settlement estimation for footings supported within compacted structural fills.

sections.title: Footings on IGMs and Rock
sections.summary: Settlement on IGMs and rock rarely governs design. When needed, use elastic theory (Eq 5-36) with Young's modulus of intact rock reduced by modulus reduction factor alpha_E = 0.0231*RQD - 1.32 (min 0.15) for rock mass quality. Shape and rigidity factors C_d from Table 5-12 account for footing geometry; intact rock modulus for 17 rock types is tabulated in Table 5-14.
sections.body:
As discussed in Section 3.1.3, the assumption is made in this GEC that intermediate geomaterials (IGMs) are stiff and strong enough that bearing capacity and settlement considerations will generally not govern design of a spread footing supported on such material. If a settlement estimate is necessary for shallow foundations supported on IGM or rock, a method based on elasticity theory will generally be the best approach. A major limitation is the engineer's ability to accurately estimate the modulus parameter(s) required by the method.

Equation 5-36 may be used to compute settlement on rock based on Young's modulus of the intact rock. The stress applied at the top of the rock surface can be calculated using the stress distribution methods shown in Figures 5-9 through 5-12. The shape and rigidity factors, C_d, are given in Table 5-12 for various footing shapes. Poisson's ratio values are summarized in Table 5-13, and Young's modulus values for intact rock are in Table 5-14. A modulus reduction factor, alpha_E, based on RQD is applied per Equation 5-37 to account for rock mass quality.

The elastic modulus of IGMs and some rocks may be measurable by in situ testing with equipment such as the pressuremeter, the flat dilatometer, plate load tests or flat jacks. Alternatively, some modulus values are available from various researchers based on rock type. Tables 5-13 and 5-14 summarize suggested values for Poisson's ratio and elastic modulus as presented in AASHTO (1996) and modified after Kulhawy (1978).

sections.title: Sliding and Lateral Stability
sections.summary: Sliding resistance is provided by base friction ((W + P_v)*tan(delta) for granular soils) or adhesion (c_a*B_f for cohesive soils). Passive resistance is conservatively ignored. Minimum FS = 1.5 against sliding for bridge foundations. Drained (Eq 5-38) and undrained (Eq 5-39) resistance equations must not be combined simultaneously.
sections.body:
A shallow foundation will resist lateral loads by a combination of the shear resistance along the base of the footing and the lateral earth pressure that develops in front of the footing in the direction of loading. The shear resistance along the base will develop its full capacity at very small deflections. The lateral earth pressure is termed 'passive resistance' and requires much larger deflections to develop the full passive capacity. By the time the passive resistance is fully developed, the shearing resistance is fully mobilized and may even by reduced to some residual value less than the peak shearing resistance. For this reason, the design of most shallow foundations conservatively ignores passive resistance.

Sliding resistance between the base of a shallow foundation and a granular soil will be governed by the coefficient of friction (tan delta) that develops between the foundation soil and the footing. The value of the coefficient of friction is a function of the soil type and the roughness of the footing. For concrete cast against cohesionless or granular material, the coefficient of friction, tan delta, will be equal to the tangent of the friction angle (tan phi) for the soil supporting the footing. If the bottom of the footing consists of something other than concrete cast against the ground, then the coefficient of friction (tan delta) is not solely a property of the soil but is also a function of the footing material type and roughness. In the absence of specific data, Table 5-15 may be used to estimate the coefficient of friction between soil and various footing material types.

If the base of the footing rests on clay, the sliding resistance will be limited by the adhesion, c_a, that develops between the bearing surface of the footing and the cohesive bearing material. In practice, c_a is typically taken as equal to the undrained shear strength (cohesion, c_u) of the clay.

The general equation for sliding resistance for footings with planar bearing surfaces on frictional (drained) materials is Equation 5-38. For cohesive (undrained) materials, the sliding resistance is given by Equation 5-39. Because drained and undrained conditions will not occur simultaneously, Equations 5-38 and 5-39 should not be combined for use at the same time.

A minimum factor of safety (FS) of 1.5 against sliding should be used for design of bridge foundations (Equation 5-40).

If sliding resistance as determined by Equation 5-39 for a footing on clay soils is insufficient, the footing width should be increased. If impractical, consideration may be given to including a key constructed under the bearing surface of the footing. The general equation for sliding resistance of footings on cohesive soils provided with a key is given by Equation 5-41. Note that in reality, keys constructed in granular soils are not very efficient in developing passive pressures; a key in granular soils is more properly considered as increasing the effective length of the shearing surface.
key_points: Passive earth pressure resistance is conservatively IGNORED in most shallow foundation designs
Sliding resistance on granular soil: F_R = (W + P_v) * tan(delta), where delta = friction angle at interface
For concrete cast against granular soil: tan(delta) = tan(phi) of the soil
Sliding resistance on clay: F_R = c_a * B_f, where c_a ~ c_u (undrained shear strength)
Minimum FS against sliding = 1.5 for bridge foundations
Do NOT combine drained (Eq 5-38) and undrained (Eq 5-39) sliding resistance
Keys in cohesive soils/soft rock can add resistance (Eq 5-41); keys in granular soils mainly increase shear surface length
Table 5-15 provides friction factors for various soil-footing material interfaces

sections.title: Global Stability
sections.summary: Global stability must be checked using limit equilibrium methods (Bishop or Spencer) when ground geometry near the footing invalidates bearing capacity theory assumptions. Footing loads can either stabilize or destabilize a nearby slope depending on their position (Figure 5-23). This check is separate from and in addition to bearing capacity and settlement analyses.
sections.body:
Global stability of shallow foundations should be evaluated when the geometry of the ground surface in any direction away from the footing suggests that the assumptions associated with the bearing capacity theory used to calculate the bearing capacity of the footing are not valid, and the stress applied by the footing loads is acting to destabilize the slope geometry. Figure 5-23 depicts slope configurations and footing locations that act to either improve or degrade the global stability of the slope.

In cases where the stress applied by the footing acts to destabilize the slope, the global stability of the footing should be checked using limit equilibrium methods such as the method of slices (Bishop, 1955; or Spencer, 1967).

Detailed guidance for the evaluation of slope stability is not included in this Circular. The Soils and Foundation Workshop Reference Manual (Cheney & Chassie, 2000) includes fundamental discussion of slope stability analysis methods considering the presence of a loaded footing within the slope. The reference work TRB Special Report 247: Landslides, Investigation and Mitigation (TRB, 1996) includes more detailed discussion on the analysis of global slope stability.
key_points: Evaluate global stability when ground geometry near the footing invalidates bearing capacity theory assumptions
Footing loads can either stabilize or destabilize a slope depending on location (Figure 5-23)
Use limit equilibrium methods (Bishop or Spencer method of slices) to check global stability
Detailed slope stability guidance is in the Soils and Foundation Workshop Reference Manual and TRB SR 247
Global stability check is separate from and additional to bearing capacity and settlement checks
